advisory.title: Unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange
advisory.description:
The client recorded the server-selected key exchange group for each server
name when processing the ServerHello, before the server was authenticated.
This record is used to predict which key share to send in future ClientHellos
to that server name.

A network attacker can answer one connection attempt with a ServerHello
selecting X25519, and then close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that
name carry only an X25519 key share, while `supported_groups` still lists
X25519MLKEM768 first. If the genuine server accepts that share rather than
sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake
completes with classical-only key exchange and no error. This persists for as
long as the entry stays in the client's session store.

The impact is loss of post-quantum confidentiality for affected connections
("harvest now, decrypt later"). There is no key compromise and no
authentication bypass.

The following are not affected:

- connections to servers which send a HelloRetryRequest for their preferred group,
- clients with resumption disabled (as nothing is stored), and
- other server names.

This behaviour is discussed in
[draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations),
so the practical impact depends largely on server policy.

advisory.title: `Debug` impls for client session values expose TLS secrets
advisory.description:
The `Debug` implementations of `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and
`Tls13ClientSessionValue` were derived, and so included the TLS 1.2 master
secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK in their output.

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations that format these values with
`Debug` (for example, when logging) could disclose these secrets to readers of
the logs. This conflicts with rustls's
[key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

Ordinary connection and built-in session cache `Debug` output is redacted and
is not affected.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Decompression bomb in `ruzstd`: a tiny input can exhaust memory (OOM)
advisory.description:
A crafted `.zst` input under 128 KB can force `ruzstd` to allocate several gigabytes at once, crashing the process with an out-of-memory condition. Since `ruzstd` is a decoder for untrusted input, a single small file is enough to take down anything decoding it.

The compressed size of a block was capped at 128 KB, but a compressed block's **decompressed** size was never checked against `Block_Maximum_Size = min(Window_Size, 128 KiB)` (RFC 8878). In `execute_sequences` the output was built with no running bound and no flush between blocks, so one block could expand to gigabytes — bypassing both the configured window-size limit and the block-by-block streaming that would otherwise release memory. (A related `u32` counter overflow on such a block caused an additional panic.)

This is a denial of service only; memory access stays in bounds (no corruption, no RCE).

`ruzstd` is also built as a dependency of the Rust standard library via `rustc-dep-of-std`; in the toolchain it is used only to load zstd-compressed debug symbols, so the toolchain-side impact is limited.

**Fixed in 0.9.1** (commit `d3907c9`), which enforces the per-block output bound. Upgrade to `ruzstd >= 0.9.1`.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

advisory.title: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` creates symbolic links whose attacker-controlled targets are outside the destination directory
advisory.description:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26

advisory.title: ZipStreamReader::extract() and ZipArchive::extract() apply Unix permissions through symlinks without confining the target
advisory.description:
`ZipStreamReader::extract()` applies Unix permissions through extracted symlinks without validating the symlink target stays within the destination

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp

advisory.title: Insecure Preservation of SUID/SGID Bits during ZIP Extraction Leading to Potential Privilege Escalation
advisory.description:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627

advisory.title: rustls-pemfile is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The rustls-pemfile crate is no longer maintained. The repository has been archived since August
2025, and users are encouraged to depend directly on the underlying PEM parsing code included
in rustls-pki-types since 1.9.0. The latest version of rustls-pemfile is in fact a thin wrapper
around the same code used in rustls-pki-types, so migrating should be straightforward.

The new API is represented by the [`PemObject`][PemObject] trait, which provides methods for
reading a single or multiple PEM objects from a file or byte slice.

[PemObject]: https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/pem/trait.PemObject.html

advisory.title: unsafe-libyaml is unmaintained
advisory.description:

its owner on 2024-03-25 and is read-only. The last release is 0.2.11
(March 2024).

`unsafe-libyaml` is a machine translation of libyaml's C code into unsafe
Rust (c2rust). Bugs found in it will not be fixed upstream. It is used by

Consider a YAML parser written in safe Rust, for example:

- [saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/saphyr) ([serde-saphyr](https://crates.io/crates/serde-saphyr) for serde users)
- [noyalib](https://crates.io/crates/noyalib)

advisory.title: Aliasing violation in `OrdSet` insertion
advisory.description:
Inserting into an `im::OrdSet` (for example by collecting an iterator into one) can violate
Rust's aliasing rules: Miri reports a stacked borrows violation in
`sized_chunks::Chunk::force_copy()`, which is called during insertion, where a shared borrow
is invalidated by a unique borrow before the read through it completes.
This is undefined behavior, reachable from safe code.

No fixed version is available, as the crate is unmaintained; its GitHub
repository was archived by the owner on 2026-05-03.

advisory.title: Unchecked pointer offset in crate `memmap2`
advisory.description:
Affected versionf of `memmap2` did not perform enough validation on the `offset` and `len` parameters of
`Mmap::[unchecked_]advise_range()`,
`MmapMut::[unchecked_]advise_ranage()`
and `MmapMut::flush[_async]_range()`.

This can cause undefined behavior due to invalid values being passed to [`pointer::offset()`] and [`pointer::add()`]
when passing an out-of-bounds range to any of the affected functions.

The flaw was corrected in commit [`cee7cf0`] and released in version `0.9.11`.

The invalid pointer is not dereferenced,
but it is passed to the `madvise` and `msync` syscalls and their Windows equivalents.

[`pointer::offset()`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.pointer.html#method.offset-1
[`pointer::add()`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.pointer.html#method.add-1
[`cee7cf0`] https://github.com/RazrFalcon/memmap2-rs/pull/170/changes/cee7cf03a9ee095982a3c37b7aac8e3f68f1a00c

advisory.title: Rand is unsound with a custom logger using `rand::rng()`
advisory.description:
It has been reported (by [@lopopolo](https://github.com/lopopolo)) that the `rand` library is [unsound](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/glossary.html#soundness-of-code--of-a-library) (i.e. that safe code using the public API can cause Undefined Behaviour) when all the following conditions are met:

- The `log` and `thread_rng` features are enabled
- A [custom logger](https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/#implementing-a-logger) is defined
- The custom logger accesses `rand::rng()` (previously `rand::thread_rng()`) and calls any `TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods on `ThreadRng`
- The `ThreadRng` (attempts to) reseed while called from the custom logger (this happens every 64 kB of generated data)
- Trace-level logging is enabled or warn-level logging is enabled and the random source (the `getrandom` crate) is unable to provide a new seed

`TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods for `ThreadRng` use `unsafe` code to cast `*mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>` to `&mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>`. When all the above conditions are met this results in an aliased mutable reference, violating the Stacked Borrows rules. Miri is able to detect this violation in sample code. Since construction of [aliased mutable references is Undefined Behaviour](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nomicon/references.html), the behaviour of optimized builds is hard to predict.

advisory.title: Panic-safety unsoundness in `Chunk`, `RingBuffer`, and `InlineArray` (use-after-free / double-free)
advisory.description:
Several methods in `sized-chunks` drop elements before updating the length/boundary metadata. If an element's `Drop` panics during the drop, the metadata update is skipped, so the container still treats the already-dropped elements as live. When the container's own `Drop` runs, those elements are visited again — a use-after-free / double-free reachable from safe Rust.

The `RingBuffer` methods require the `ringbuffer` feature. This is distinct from RUSTSEC-2020-0041 (`Chunk::clone` / `insert_from`, fixed in 0.6.3); the methods here are still affected in 0.7.0. The repository is archived with issues/PRs disabled and no fix available.

## Impact

- **CWE-415 (Double Free):** the same allocation is freed twice.
- **CWE-416 (Use-After-Free):** a freed allocation is accessed during a repeated `Drop`.

Reachable entirely from safe Rust via `catch_unwind` with element types whose `Drop` can panic.
